text: The density $ρ$ of a uniform cylinder is determined by measuring its mass $m$, length $l$ and diameter $d$. The measured values of $m,l$ and $d$ are $97.42\pm 0.02\mathrm{g}$, $8.35\pm 0.05\mathrm{mm}$ and $20.20\pm 0.02\mathrm{mm}$, respectively. Calculated percentage fractional error in $ρ$ is $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The density $(ρ)$ of a body is defined as the ratio of its mass (m) to its volume (V).

$ρ=\frac{m}{V}$

For a uniform cylinder of length l and diameter D , the volume is,

$V=πr^{2}l=π\left (\frac{D}{2}\right )^{2}l=\frac{πD^{2}l}{4}$

Substituting the volume into the density formula:

$ρ=\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{V}}=\frac{4\mathrm{m}}{π\mathrm{D}^{2}\mathrm{l}}$

To find the fractional error, we take the natural logarithm $(\ln )$ on both sides:

$\ln (ρ)=\ln (4)+\ln (m)-\ln (π)-2\ln (D)-\ln (l)$

Differentiating both sides to find the relative change

$\frac{\mathrm{d}ρ}{ρ}=\frac{\mathrm{dm}}{\mathrm{m}}-\frac{2\mathrm{dD}}{\mathrm{D}}-\frac{\mathrm{dl}}{\mathrm{l}}$

The maximum possible fractional error is the sum of the absolute values of the individual relative errors:

$\frac{\Delta ρ}{ρ}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{m}}+\frac{2\Delta \mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{D}}+\frac{\Delta \mathrm{l}}{\mathrm{l}}$

For the percentage fractional error,

$%\text{Error in}ρ=\left (\frac{\Delta \mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{m}}+\frac{2\Delta \mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{D}}+\frac{\Delta \mathrm{l}}{\mathrm{l}}\right )\times 100$

The measured value of mass is $97.42\pm 0.02\mathrm{g}\Rightarrow \mathrm{m}=97.42\mathrm{g}$ and the absolute error is $\Delta \mathrm{m}=0.02\mathrm{g}$ So, relative error in mass is,

$\frac{\Delta \mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{0.02}{97.42}\approx 0.000205$

The measured value of length is $8.35\pm 0.05\mathrm{mm}\Rightarrow \mathrm{l}=8.35\mathrm{mm}$ and the absolute error is $\Delta \mathrm{l}=0.05\mathrm{mm}$ 

So, relative error in length is,

$\frac{\Delta \mathrm{l}}{\mathrm{l}}=\frac{0.05}{8.35}\approx 0.005988$

The measured value of diameter is $20.20\pm 0.02\mathrm{mm}\Rightarrow \mathrm{D}=20.20\mathrm{mm}$ and the absolute error is $\Delta \mathrm{D}=$ 0.02 mm

So, relative error in diameter is,

$\frac{2\Delta \mathrm{D}}{\mathrm{D}}=\frac{2\times 0.02}{20.20}=\frac{0.04}{20.20}\approx 0.001980$

Putting the values in the expression for the percentage error in density,

$\frac{\Delta ρ}{ρ}\times 100%=(0.000205+0.005988+0.001980)\times 100%=0.008173\times 100%$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\Delta ρ}{ρ}\times 100%=0.8173%\approx 0.82%$

Therefore, the calculated percentage fraction error in density is approximately $0.82%$. 

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text: The potential energy of a particle changes with distance $x$ from a fixed origin as $V=\frac{A\sqrt{x}}{x+B}$, where $A$ and $B$ are constants with appropriate dimensions. The dimensions of $AB$ are $____$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
According to the principle of homogeneity, dimensions of each term on both sides of an equation must be the same. Also, only physical quantities of the same dimensions can be added or subtracted.

The potential energy of the particle is given as $V=\frac{A\sqrt{x}}{x+B}$, where $A$ and $B$ are constant.

In the denominator of the expression $\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{B}$, the constant B is added to distance x . Therefore, the dimensions of $B$ must be the same as the dimensions of $x$.

$[\mathrm{B}]=[\mathrm{x}]=\left [\mathrm{L}^{1}\right ]$

The potential energy $V$ has the same dimensions as work or energy.

$[\mathrm{V}]=[\mathrm{F}\times \mathrm{x}]=\left [\mathrm{M}^{1}\mathrm{L}^{1}\mathrm{T}^{-2}\times \mathrm{L}^{1}\right ]=\left [\mathrm{M}^{1}\mathrm{L}^{2}\mathrm{T}^{-2}\right ]$

On rearranging the formula of potential energy for A :

$A=\frac{V(x+B)}{\sqrt{x}}$

Substituting the dimensions:

$[\mathrm{A}]=\frac{\left [\mathrm{M}^{1}\mathrm{L}^{2}\mathrm{T}^{-2}\right ]\left [\mathrm{L}^{1}\right ]}{\left [\mathrm{L}^{1/2}\right ]}$

$\Rightarrow$ $[\mathrm{A}]=\frac{\left [\mathrm{M}^{1}\mathrm{L}^{3}\mathrm{T}^{-2}\right ]}{\left [\mathrm{L}^{1/2}\right ]}$

$\Rightarrow[\mathrm{A}]=\left [\mathrm{M}^{1}\mathrm{L}^{3-\frac{1}{2}}\mathrm{T}^{-2}\right ]=\left [\mathrm{M}^{1}\mathrm{L}^{5/2}\mathrm{T}^{-2}\right ]$

To find the dimensions of the product AB :

$[\mathrm{AB}]=[\mathrm{A}]\times [\mathrm{B}]$

$\Rightarrow$ $[\mathrm{AB}]=\left [\mathrm{M}^{1}\mathrm{L}^{5/2}\mathrm{T}^{-2}\right ]\times \left [\mathrm{L}^{1}\right ]$

$\Rightarrow$ $[\mathrm{AB}]=\left [\mathrm{M}^{1}\mathrm{L}^{5/2+1}\mathrm{T}^{-2}\right ]$

$\Rightarrow$ $[\mathrm{AB}]=\left [\mathrm{M}^{1}\mathrm{L}^{7/2}\mathrm{T}^{-2}\right ]$

Therefore, the dimensions of $AB$ is $\left [M^{1}L^{7/2}T^{-2}\right ]$. 

Thus, the correct option is (D).

text:
The rain drop of mass 1 g , starts with zero velocity from a height of 1 km . It hits the ground with a speed of $5\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$. The work done by the unknown resistive force is $____$ J.

(take $\mathrm{g}=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The Work-Energy Theorem states that the total work done by all forces (conservative and non-conservative) on a particle is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.

$\mathrm{W}_{\text{total}}=\Delta \mathrm{K}$

When rain drop is falling, it experiences gravitational force (vertically downward) and resistive force which opposes motion of rain drop (vertically upward).


[IMG]


$\mathrm{W}_{\text{gravity}}+\mathrm{W}_{\text{resistive}}=\mathrm{K}_{\text{final}}-\mathrm{K}_{\text{initial}}$

Work done by gravity when an object falls a height h is:

$\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{g}}=\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{g}}\mathrm{h}=\mathrm{mgh}$

The mass of the rain drop is $\mathrm{m}=1\mathrm{g}=1\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{kg}$

The height of drop is $\mathrm{h}=1\mathrm{km}=1000\mathrm{m}$

And the acceleration due to gravity is $\mathrm{g}=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$

Putting the values,

$W_{g}=\left (10^{-3}\right )\times (10)\times (1000)=10\mathrm{J}$

The initial velocity is $u=0$ as it started from rest, so the initial kinetic energy is $K_{\text{initial}}=\frac{1}{2}mu^{2}=0$.

The final velocity when rain drop hits the ground is $\mathrm{v}=5\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}$.

Thus, the final kinetic energy of the rain drop is

$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{final}}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{mv}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $K_{final}=\frac{1}{2}\times \left (10^{-3}\right )\times (5)^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{K}_{\text{final}}=\frac{1}{2}\times 10^{-3}\times 25=12.5\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{J}=0.0125\mathrm{J}$

Using the work-energy theorem equation,

$\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{g}}+\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{r}}=\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{final}}-\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{initial}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $10\mathrm{J}+\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{r}}=0.0125\mathrm{J}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{r}}=0.0125-10$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{r}}=-9.9875\mathrm{J}$

Therefore, the magnitude of the work done by the resistive force is approximately 9.98 J . 

Thus, the correct option is (D).

text:
Two blocks ( $P$ and $Q$ ) with respectively masses 2 kg and 1.5 kg are joined by a massless thread. These blocks are mounted on a frictionless pulley which is fixed on the edge of a cube $(S)$, as shown in the figure below. Block $P$ is positioned on the top surface which has no friction and block $Q$ is in contact with side-surface, having coefficient friction $μ$. The cube ( $S$ ) moves towards the right with acceleration of $\frac{g}{2}$, where $g$ is gravitational acceleration. During this movement the block $P$ and $Q$ remain stationary. The value of $μ$ is $____$ (take $\mathrm{g}=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$ )

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Since the cube is accelerating at $\mathrm{a}=\frac{\mathrm{g}}{2}$ to the right, when analysing the blocks from the cube's non-inertial frame, we must apply a pseudo-force ( $\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{m}\times \mathrm{a}$ ) on both blocks in the opposite direction to the acceleration of block S.

[IMG]

For block P (Mass $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{P}}=2\mathrm{kg}$ )
Along horizontal the tension (T) in the thread pulls it to the right. The pseudo-force ( $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{P}}\cdot \mathrm{a}$ ) pulls it to the left. Along vertical direction gravity ( $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{P}}\mathrm{g}$ ) acts downward and normal force ( $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{P}}$ ) from the top surface acts upward. Since the block is stationary relative to the cube :
$\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{P}}\cdot \mathrm{a}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{P}}\cdot \frac{\mathrm{g}}{2}$
$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{T}=2\times \frac{10}{2}=10\mathrm{N}$
For block Q (Mass $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{Q}}=1.5\mathrm{kg}$ )
Along horizontal direction the cube pushes against the block with a normal force $(\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{Q}})$ to the right. The pseudoforce $(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{Q}}\cdot \mathrm{a})$ acts to the left.
$\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{Q}}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{Q}}\cdot \mathrm{a}=1.5\times \frac{\mathrm{g}}{2}$
Along vertical direction, gravity ( $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{Q}}\mathrm{g}$ ) acts downward.
$\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{gQ}}=1.5\times 10=15\mathrm{N}$
Tension (T) in the thread acts upward, $\mathrm{T}=10\mathrm{N}$ [as the string is massless and inextensible]
Friction (f) acts upward to prevent the block from falling.
For equilibrium in the vertical direction:
$\mathrm{T}+\mathrm{f}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{Q}}\mathrm{g}$
$\Rightarrow$ $10+\mathrm{f}=15\Rightarrow \mathrm{f}=5\mathrm{N}$
The friction force is given by $\mathrm{f}=μ\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{Q}}$.
$5=μ\times \left (1.5\times \frac{10}{2}\right )$
$\Rightarrow$ $5=μ\times (1.5\times 5)$
$\Rightarrow$ $5=μ\times 7.5$
$\Rightarrow$ $μ=\frac{5}{7.5}=\frac{2}{3}\approx 0.67$
Therefore, the value of coefficient of friction between the block Q and S is $μ=0.67$.
Thus, the correct option is (B).

text:
A lift of mass 1600 kg is supported by thick iron wire. If the maximum stress which the wire can withstand is $4\times 10^{8}\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m}^{2}$ and its radius is 4 mm , then maximum acceleration the lift can take is $____$ $\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$.

(take $\mathrm{g}=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$ and $π=3.14$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
When a lift of mass M accelerates upward with acceleration a, the tension (T) in the supporting cable must overcome both gravity and provide the upward acceleration.


[IMG]


Using Newton's Second Law ( $\mathrm{F}_{\text{net}}=\mathrm{Ma}$ ):

$\mathrm{T}-\mathrm{Mg}=\mathrm{Ma}\Rightarrow \mathrm{T}=\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{g}+\mathrm{a})$

The stress $(σ)$ is defined as the restoring force (tension) per unit cross-sectional area (A):

$σ=\frac{T}{A}=\frac{M(g+a)}{A}$

For a wire with a circular cross-section of radius r , the area of cross-section is $\mathrm{A}=π\mathrm{r}^{2}$.

$σ_{\max }=\frac{\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{g}+\mathrm{a}_{\max })}{π\mathrm{r}^{2}}$

The mass of lift is $\mathrm{M}=1600\mathrm{kg}$

The radius of cable is $\mathrm{r}=4\mathrm{mm}=4\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{m}$

So, the area is

$\mathrm{A}=π\mathrm{r}^{2}=3.14\times \left (4\times 10^{-3}\right )^{2}=3.14\times 16\times 10^{-6}\mathrm{m}^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{A}=50.24\times 10^{-6}\mathrm{m}^{2}$

So, the maximum stress is

$σ_{\max }=4\times 10^{8}\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m}^{2}$

From the maximum stress formula,

$4\times 10^{8}=\frac{1600(10+\mathrm{a}_{\max })}{50.24\times 10^{-6}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $4\times 10^{8}\times 50.24\times 10^{-6}=1600(10+a_{\max })$

$\Rightarrow$ $200.96\times 10^{2}=1600(10+a_{\max })$

$\Rightarrow$ $20096=1600(10+a_{\max })$

$\Rightarrow$ $10+a_{\max }=\frac{20096}{1600}=12.56$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{a}_{\max }=12.56-10=2.56\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$

Therefore, the maximum acceleration of the lift is $2.56\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$. 

Thus, the correct option is (A).

text: A solid sphere of radius 4 cm and mass 5 kg is rotating (rotation axis is passing through the centre of the sphere) with an angular velocity of 1200 rpm . It is brought to rest in 10 s by applying a constant torque. The torque applied and the number of rotations it made before it comes to rest are $____$ and $____$ respectively.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The mass of the solid sphere is $M=5\mathrm{kg}$ and its radius is $R=4\mathrm{cm}=0.04\mathrm{m}$


[IMG]


For a solid sphere rotating about its centre, the moment of inertia is $I=\frac{2}{5}MR^{2}$

$I=\frac{2}{5}\times 5\times (0.04)^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{I}=2\times 0.0016=0.0032\mathrm{kg}\cdot \mathrm{m}^{2}$

The initial angular velocity is $ω_{0}=1200\mathrm{rpm}$ (rotations per minute).

The rate of rotation, usually measured in radians per second $\left (\frac{\mathrm{rad}}{\mathrm{s}}\right )$.

$ω_{0}=2π\times \frac{1200}{60}=40π\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}$

The final angular velocity is $ω=0$

The time taken before it comes to rest is $\mathrm{t}=10\mathrm{s}$.

Using the rotational kinematic equation,

$ω=ω_{0}+αt$

$\Rightarrow$ $0=40π+α(10)$

$\Rightarrow$ $α=-\frac{40π}{10}=-4π\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$

The negative sign shows the solid sphere is slowing down.

Using the law of rotational motion, $τ=\mathrm{I}α$, where $τ$ is the torque acting and $α$ is the resultant angular acceleration.

$τ=I\times |α|$

$\Rightarrow$ $τ=0.0032\times 4π=0.0128π\mathrm{Nm}$

Using kinematic equation for rotational motion $θ=ω_{0}\mathrm{t}+\frac{1}{2}α\mathrm{t}^{2}$, the total angle covered is,

$θ=40π\times 10+\frac{1}{2}\times (-4π)\times 10^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $θ=400π-2π\times 100=200π\text{radians}$

Since one full rotation is $2π$ radians, the number of rotations is:

$\mathrm{N}=\frac{θ}{2π}=\frac{200π}{2π}=100\text{rotations}$

Therefore, the magnitude of applied torque is $0.0128π\mathrm{Nm}$ and the number of rotations is 100 . Thus, the correct option is (D).

text:
A smooth inclined plane ends in a vertical circular loop, as shown in the figure. A small body is released from height $h$ as shown. If the body exerts a force of three times its weight on the plane at the highest point of circle then the height $h=αR$. The value of $α$ is $____$


[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The potential energy at height $h$ converts into kinetic energy as the object slides down.

To move in a circle of radius $R$, the net force toward the center must be $\frac{mv^{2}}{R}$.

Let the bottom of the loop be the reference level (Potential Energy $=0$ ).


[IMG]


At release point, the gravitational potential energy is $\mathrm{PE}_{1}=\mathrm{mgh}$, and the kinetic energy is $\mathrm{KE}_{1}=0$.

So, total energy of the body at releasing point is $\mathrm{E}_{1}=\mathrm{PE}_{1}+\mathrm{KE}_{1}=\mathrm{mgh}+0=\mathrm{mgh}$

At the highest point of circle the height is 2 R (the diameter).

So, the gravitational potential energy is $\mathrm{PE}_{2}=\mathrm{mg}(2\mathrm{R})$.

Let velocity at the top be $\mathrm{v}_{2}$. So, the kinetic energy of body at top is $\mathrm{KE}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{mv}_{2}^{2}$.

So, the total energy of the body at top of the circle is $\mathrm{E}_{2}=2\mathrm{mgR}+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{mv}_{2}^{2}$.

Using law of conservation of energy :

$\mathrm{mgh}=2\mathrm{mgR}+\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{mv}_{2}^{2}$

$gh=2gR+\frac{v_{2}^{2}}{2}\Rightarrow v_{2}^{2}=2g(h-2R)\ldots (i)$

At the top of the loop, normal force ( N ) acts on the body from the track.

It is given that the body exerts a force of 3 mg on the plane, so by Newton's 3rd Law, the track exerts $\mathrm{N}=3\mathrm{mg}$ on the body.

So, total centripetal force is $\mathrm{N}+\mathrm{mg}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}_{2}^{2}}{\mathrm{R}}$

Substituting N = 3mg:

$3\mathrm{mg}+\mathrm{mg}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}_{2}^{2}}{\mathrm{R}}\Rightarrow 4\mathrm{mg}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}_{2}^{2}}{\mathrm{R}}$

$\mathrm{v}_{2}^{2}=4\mathrm{gR}\ldots \text{(ii)}$

From both the equations,

$2\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{h}-2\mathrm{R})=4\mathrm{gR}$

$\Rightarrow$ $h-2R=2R$

$\Rightarrow$ $h=4R=αR\Rightarrow α=4$

Therefore, the value of $α$ is 4 . Thus, the correct option is (B).

text:
The position of center of mass of three masses $2\mathrm{kg},3\mathrm{kg}$ and 15 kg placed with respect to mid point $(p)$ of normal bisector, as shown in the figure is $____$ .

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
If we have multiple masses $\mathrm{m}_{1},\mathrm{m}_{2},\ldots$ at positions $(\mathrm{x}_{1},\mathrm{y}_{1}),(\mathrm{x}_{2},\mathrm{y}_{2}),\ldots$, the coordinates of the COM are

$\begin{array}{ll} \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{cm}} & =\dfrac{\mathrm{m}_{1}\mathrm{x}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}\mathrm{x}_{2}+\mathrm{m}_{3}\mathrm{x}_{3}\ldots }{\mathrm{m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}+\mathrm{m}_{3}\ldots } \\ \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{cm}} & =\dfrac{\mathrm{m}_{1}\mathrm{y}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}\mathrm{y}_{2}+\mathrm{m}_{3}\mathrm{y}_{3}\ldots }{\mathrm{m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}+\mathrm{m}_{3}\ldots } \end{array}$

Let the midpoint p be the origin $(0,0)$. From the geometry,


[IMG]


In right angled triangle $\mathrm{ACD},\cos 60^{\circ }=\frac{\mathrm{CD}}{\mathrm{AC}}\Rightarrow \mathrm{CD}=\mathrm{AC}\cos 60^{\circ }=10\times \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{m}=5\mathrm{m}$

Point P is the midpoint of CD , so $\mathrm{PC}=\mathrm{PD}=\frac{\mathrm{CD}}{2}=\frac{5\mathrm{m}}{2}=2.5\mathrm{m}$

As P is the origin, the coordinate of 15 kg is $(0,2.5)\mathrm{m}$ and the coordinates of D is $(0,-2.5)\mathrm{m}$.

As 2 kg and 3 kg is on the same horizontal level as D, so y-coordinate of 2 kg and 3 kg is $\mathrm{y}_{1}=-2.5\mathrm{m}$

Also, $\sin 60^{\circ }=\frac{\mathrm{AD}}{10}\Rightarrow \mathrm{AD}=10\sin 60^{\circ }=10\times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}=5\sqrt{3}\mathrm{m}$

Hence, the $x$-coordinate of 2 kg is $-5\sqrt{3}\mathrm{m}$ and that of 3 kg it is $5\sqrt{3}\mathrm{m}$

Hence, the coordinates of 2 kg are $(-5\sqrt{3},-2.5)$, the coordinate of 3 kg are $(5\sqrt{3},-2.5)$, and that of 15 kg is (0,2.5).

The total mass of system is $\mathrm{M}=2+3+15=20\mathrm{kg}$.

So, the x -coordinate of centre of mass is:

$\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{(15\times (0))+(3\times 5\sqrt{3})+(2\times (-5\sqrt{3}))}{20}=\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{20}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$

And the y -coordinate of centre of mass is:

$y_{cm}=\frac{(15\times 2.5)+(3\times (-2.5))+(2\times (-2.5))}{20}=\frac{37.5-12.5}{20}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{25}{20}=\frac{5}{4}=1.25$

Therefore, the centre of mass of system of masses is $\left (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4},1.25\right )$. 

Hence, the correct option is (A).

text:
The two wires $A$ and $B$ of equal cross-section but of different materials are joined together. The ratio of Young's modulus of wire $A$ and wire $B$ is 20/11. When the joined wire is kept under certain tension the elongations in the wires $A$ and $B$ are equal. If the length of wire $A$ is 2.2 m , then the length of wire $B$ is

$____$ m.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Young's Modulus is defined as the ratio of Stress $(σ)$ to Strain $(𝜖)$.

$Y=\frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}}=\frac{σ}{𝜖}$

Stress is force per unit area, $σ=\frac{\text{Force (F)}}{\text{Area (A)}}$

Strain is change in length per unit original length,

$𝜖=\frac{\text{Change in length}(\Delta \mathrm{L})}{\text{Original length}(\mathrm{L})}$

So, $Y=\frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L}$

$\Rightarrow \Delta \mathrm{L}=\frac{\mathrm{FL}}{\mathrm{AY}}$

Since the wires are joined in series and kept under tension, the Force (F) acting on both wires is the same.

The area (A) is the same for both.

It is given that the elongation in both the wires is equal, $\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}=\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}$.

Since $\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}=\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}:$

$\frac{FL_{A}}{AY_{A}}=\frac{FL_{B}}{AY_{B}}$

$\Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{A}}}=\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{B}}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{B}}}$

The ratio of Young's modulus is $\frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=\frac{20}{11}$ and the length of wire $A$ is $L_{A}=2.2\mathrm{m}$

$\frac{2.2}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{20}{11}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}=2.2\times \frac{11}{20}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{24.2}{20}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}=1.21\mathrm{m}$

Therefore, the length of wire B is 1.21 m . Hence, the correct option is (C).

text: Two closed vessels of same volume are joined through a narrow tube and both vessels are filled with air of pressure 90 kPa and temperature 400 K . Keeping the temperature of one vessel constant at 400 K the second vessel temperature is raised to 500 K . The final pressure in the vessels is $____$ kPa .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Using Ideal Gas Law:

PV = nRT

Where P is pressure, V is volume, n is number of moles, R is the gas constant, and T is absolute temperature. Since the system is closed, the total number of moles ( $\mathrm{n}_{\text{total}}$ ) remains constant before and after heating.

Initial State:

Both vessels (each of volume V ) are at $\mathrm{P}_{0}=90\mathrm{kPa}$ and $\mathrm{T}_{0}=400\mathrm{K}$.

$\mathrm{n}_{\text{total}}=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{0}\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{RT}_{0}}+\frac{\mathrm{P}_{0}\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{RT}_{0}}=\frac{2\mathrm{P}_{0}\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{RT}_{0}}\ldots (i)$

Final State: Pressure becomes $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}$ in both vessels. Vessel 1 stays at $\mathrm{T}_{1}=400\mathrm{K}$, and vessel 2 is at $\mathrm{T}_{2}=500\mathrm{K}$.

$\mathrm{n}_{\text{total}}=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{RT}_{1}}+\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{RT}_{2}}=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{R}}\left (\frac{1}{\mathrm{T}_{1}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{T}_{2}}\right )\ldots (ii)$

From both the equations,

$\frac{2\mathrm{P}_{0}\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{RT}_{0}}=\frac{\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{R}}\left (\frac{1}{\mathrm{T}_{1}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{T}_{2}}\right )\Rightarrow \frac{2\mathrm{P}_{0}}{\mathrm{T}_{0}}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}\left (\frac{1}{\mathrm{T}_{1}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{T}_{2}}\right )$

Substituting the values ( $\mathrm{P}_{0}=90,\mathrm{T}_{0}=400,\mathrm{T}_{1}=400,\mathrm{T}_{2}=500$ ):

$2\times \frac{90}{400}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}\left (\frac{1}{400}+\frac{1}{500}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{180}{400}=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}\left (\frac{5+4}{2000}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $0.45=\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{f}}\left (\frac{9}{2000}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $P_{f}=\frac{0.45\times 2000}{9}=\frac{900}{9}=100\mathrm{kPa}$

Therefore, the final pressure of the vessel is 100 kPa . Thus, the correct option is (A).

text: In interference experiment the path difference between two interfering waves at a point $A$ on the screen is $λ/3$, where $λ$ is the wavelength of these waves, and at another point $B$ the path difference is $λ/6$. The ratio of intensities at points $A$ and $B$ is $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The relation between phase difference $(𝜙)$ and path difference $(\Delta x)$ is:

$𝜙=\frac{2π}{λ}\Delta x$

For two waves of equal intensity $\mathrm{I}_{0}$, the resultant intensity I at a point is:

$\mathrm{I}=4\mathrm{I}_{0}\cos ^{2}\left (\frac{𝜙}{2}\right )$

At point A the path difference is $\Delta \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{λ}{3}$.

$𝜙_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{2π}{λ}\times \frac{λ}{3}=\frac{2π}{3}$

So, the resultant intensity at A is,

$I_{A}=4I_{0}\cos ^{2}\left (\frac{2π/3}{2}\right )=4I_{0}\cos ^{2}\left (\frac{π}{3}\right )=4I_{0}\left (\frac{1}{2}\right )^{2}=I_{0}$

At point B the path difference is $\Delta \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{λ}{6}$.

$𝜙_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{2π}{λ}\times \frac{λ}{6}=\frac{π}{3}$

So, the resultant intensity at B is,

$I_{B}=4I_{0}\cos ^{2}\left (\frac{π/3}{2}\right )=4I_{0}\cos ^{2}\left (\frac{π}{6}\right )=4I_{0}\left (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right )^{2}=3I_{0}$

So, the ratio of intensities at A and B is;

$\frac{\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\frac{\mathrm{I}_{0}}{3\mathrm{I}_{0}}=\frac{1}{3}$

Thus, the correct option is (C).

text: A particle is executing simple harmonic motion. Its amplitude is $A$ and time period is 5 sec . The time required by it to move from $x=A$ to $x=\frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$ is $____$ sec.

solution.body:
For a particle starting from the extreme position $(x=A)$ at $t=0$, the displacement $x$ at any time $t$ is given by:

$x=A\cos (ωt)$

Where $ω$ is the angular frequency, defined as $ω=\frac{2π}{\mathrm{T}}$.

The given time period is $\mathrm{T}=5\sec$ :

$ω=\frac{2π}{5}\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}$


[IMG]


The particle moves to $\mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{A}}{\sqrt{2}}$. Substituting into the displacement equation:

$\frac{\mathrm{A}}{\sqrt{2}}=\mathrm{A}\cos \left (\frac{2π}{5}\mathrm{t}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\cos \left (\frac{2π}{5}t\right )$

Since $\cos \left (\frac{π}{4}\right )=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ :

$\frac{π}{4}=\frac{2π}{5}\mathrm{t}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{t}=\frac{5}{8}\sec$

Therefore, the correct option is (C).

A thin half ring of radius 35 cm is uniformly charged with a total charge of $Q$ coulomb. If the magnitude of the electric field at centre of the half ring is $100\mathrm{V}/\mathrm{m}$, then the value of $Q$ is $____$ nC .

$\left (𝜖_{0}=8.85\times 10^{-12}\mathrm{C}^{2}/\mathrm{Nm}^{2}\text{and}π=3.14\right )$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For a uniformly charged semicircular ring with linear charge density $λ$ and radius R , the electric field E at the center is:

$E=\frac{2\mathrm{k}λ}{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{2λ}{4π𝜖_{0}\mathrm{R}}=\frac{λ}{2π𝜖_{0}\mathrm{R}}$

Where $λ=\frac{\text{Total Charge}}{\text{Length}}=\frac{\mathrm{Q}}{π\mathrm{R}}$.

Substituting $λ$ into the field formula:

$E=\frac{Q/πR}{2π𝜖_{0}R}=\frac{Q}{2π^{2}𝜖_{0}R^{2}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{E}\cdot 2π^{2}𝜖_{0}\mathrm{R}^{2}$

The magnitude of electric field at the centre is $\mathrm{E}=100\mathrm{V}/\mathrm{m}$

The radius of the semi-circle is $\mathrm{R}=35\mathrm{cm}=0.35\mathrm{m}$

The value of $𝜖_{0}=8.85\times 10^{-12}$ and $π=3.14$

$Q=100\times 2\times (3.14)^{2}\times 8.85\times 10^{-12}\times (0.35)^{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $Q=100\times 2\times 9.8596\times 8.85\times 10^{-12}\times 0.1225$

$\Rightarrow$ $Q\approx 2.14\times 10^{-9}C$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{Q}=2.14\mathrm{nC}$

Therefore, the value of Q is 2.14 nC . Thus, the correct option is (A).

The maximum rated power of the LED is 2 mW and it is used in the circuit with input voltage of 5 V as shown in the figure below. The current through resistance $R_{S}$ is 0.5 mA .

The minimum value of the resistance of $R_{S}$, to ensure that the LED is not damaged is $____$ $\mathrm{k}\Omega$.

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The input voltage is $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{s}}=5\mathrm{V}$.

The total current in shunt resistance is $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{s}}=0.5\mathrm{mA}=0.5\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{A}$.

The power rating of LED is $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{LED}}=2\mathrm{mW}=2\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{W}$.

The resistance added parallel to LED is R $=1\mathrm{k}\Omega =1000\Omega$.

As the diode in branch containing $R$ is in reverse biased, so current through it is zero. Hence, the current through LED is same as that through $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{S}},\mathrm{I}_{\text{LED}}=0.5\mathrm{mA}=0.5\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{A}$

The power rating of LED is $2\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{W}$,

Since $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{R}}\times \mathrm{R}$, we have $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}}{1000}$.

To find the maximum safe operating voltage for the LED, we use the power formula:

$\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{V}\times \mathrm{I}$

The power consumed by the LED is $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{LED}}=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}\times \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{LED}}$.

$2\times 10^{-3}=V_{L}\times 0.5\times 10^{-3}\Rightarrow V_{L}=4V$

From the circuit, the voltage drop across $R_{S}$ is $V_{R_{S}}=V_{S}-V_{L}$.

$V_{R_{S}}=5\mathrm{V}-4\mathrm{V}=1\mathrm{V}$

By Ohm's Law $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{S}}=\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{R}\mathrm{S}}}{\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{s}}}=\frac{1}{0.5\times 10^{-3}}=2\times 10^{3}\Omega =2\mathrm{k}\Omega$

Therefore, the minimum value of the resistance $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{S}}$ to ensure that LED is not damaged is $2\mathrm{k}\Omega$. Thus, the correct option is (B).

text: A point light source emits E.M. waves in free space. A detector, placed at a distance of $L\mathrm{m}$, measures the intensity as $I_{\mathrm{o}}$. The detector is now shifted to another location on the same spherical surface ensuring the angle between original location and new location as $45^{\circ }$. The measured intensity at new location will be $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The intensity (I) of electromagnetic waves from a point source in free space follows the inverse square law.

$I=\frac{P}{4πr^{2}}$

Where P is the power of the source and r is the distance from the source.


[IMG]


Initial distance is L and the intensity recorded is $\mathrm{I}_{0}$.

It is given that the detector is shifted to another location on the same spherical surface.

On a spherical surface, all points are at a constant distance r from the center (the source).

Since the detector remains on the same spherical surface, its distance from the point source remains L .

The angle ( $45^{\circ }$ ) represents a change in direction, but not a change in distance r .

As r is constant $\mathrm{r}_{1}=\mathrm{r}_{2}=\mathrm{L}$ :

$I_{\text{new}}=\frac{P}{4πL^{2}}=I_{0}$

Therefore, the measured intensity at new location will be $\mathrm{I}_{0}$. Hence, the correct option is (B).

text:
A spherical interface lens of radius $R$ separates two media of refractive indices 1 and 1.4 respectively as shown in the figure below. A point source is placed at a distance of $4R$ in front of spherical interface. The magnitude of the magnification of point source image is $____$ .

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
When light travels from one medium to another through a curved surface, the positions of the object ( $u$ ) and the image (v) are related by the formula:

$\frac{\mathrm{n}_{2}}{\mathrm{v}}-\frac{\mathrm{n}_{1}}{\mathrm{u}}=\frac{\mathrm{n}_{2}-\mathrm{n}_{1}}{\mathrm{R}}$

Where $\mathrm{n}_{1}$ is the refractive index of the medium where the object is placed, $\mathrm{n}_{2}$ is the refractive index of the medium where light enters, R is the radius of curvature.

The refractive index of medium in which object is $\mathrm{n}_{1}=1$, and that for the image $\mathrm{n}_{2}=1.4$.

The object distance is $u=-4R$ (as per sign convention), and radius is $+R$ (convex surface).

$\frac{1.4}{v}-\frac{1}{-4R}=\frac{1.4-1}{R}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1.4}{v}+\frac{1}{4R}=\frac{0.4}{R}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{1.4}{v}=\frac{0.4}{R}-\frac{0.25}{R}=\frac{0.15}{R}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{v}=\frac{1.4\mathrm{R}}{0.15}=\frac{140\mathrm{R}}{15}=\frac{28}{3}\mathrm{R}$

For a spherical refracting interface, the magnification is given by :

$\mathrm{m}=\frac{\mathrm{n}_{1}\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{n}_{2}\mathrm{u}}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{m}=\frac{1\times \left (\frac{28}{3}\mathrm{R}\right )}{1.4\times (-4\mathrm{R})}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{m}=\frac{28\mathrm{R}/3}{-5.6\mathrm{R}}=\frac{28}{3\times (-5.6)}=\frac{28}{-16.8}$

$\Rightarrow$ $|\mathrm{m}|=\frac{28}{16.8}=1.666\ldots$

Therefore, the magnitude of the magnification of point source image is 1.66 . 

Thus, the correct option is (A).

text:
A small cube of side 1 mm is placed at the centre of a circular loop of radius 10 cm carrying a current of 2 A . The magnetic energy stored inside the cube is $α\times 10^{-14}\mathrm{J}$. The value of $α$ is $____$ .

$\left (μ_{\mathrm{o}}=4π\times 10^{-7}\mathrm{Tm}/\mathrm{A},π=3.14\right )$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The magnetic field produced at the center of a circular wire of radius $r$ carrying current $I$ is:

$B=\frac{μ_{0}I}{2r}$

The electric current in the circular loop is $\mathrm{I}=2\mathrm{A}$, the radius of the loop is $\mathrm{r}=10\mathrm{cm}=0.1\mathrm{m}$.

$\mathrm{B}=\frac{4π\times 10^{-7}\times 2}{2\times 0.1}=4π\times 10^{-6}\mathrm{T}$

Magnetic energy is stored in the space where a magnetic field exists. The energy per unit volume is:

$u_{B}=\frac{B^{2}}{2μ_{0}}$

For a very small volume V where the field B is approximately uniform:

$\mathrm{U}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{B}}\times \mathrm{V}=\frac{\mathrm{B}^{2}}{2μ_{0}}\times \mathrm{V}$

The volume of the cube is,

$V=(1\mathrm{mm})^{3}=\left (10^{-3}\mathrm{m}\right )^{3}=10^{-9}\mathrm{m}^{3}$

So, the total energy stored in the cube is,

$U=\frac{\left (4π\times 10^{-6}\right )^{2}}{2\times 4π\times 10^{-7}}\times 10^{-9}$

$\Rightarrow$ $U=\frac{16π^{2}\times 10^{-12}}{8π\times 10^{-7}}\times 10^{-9}=2π\times 10^{-5}\times 10^{-9}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{U}=2\times 3.14\times 10^{-14}=6.28\times 10^{-14}\mathrm{J}=α\times 10^{-14}\mathrm{J}$

$\Rightarrow α=6.28$

Therefore, the correct option is (A).

When a battery is connected to an inductor $(\mathrm{L})$ and a resistor $(\mathrm{R})$ in series, the total voltage $(\mathrm{E})$ provided by the battery is shared between the resistance and the inductance according to Kirchhoff's Voltage Law:

Where, E is the E.M.F. of the battery. $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{R}}$ is the voltage across the resistance, calculated as $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{R}}=\mathrm{iR}.\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{L}}$ is the instantaneous voltage across the inductor.

The emf of the battery is $\mathrm{E}=1.0\mathrm{V}$ and connected resistance is $\mathrm{R}=100\Omega$.

Case 1 when the current passing through inductor is $\mathrm{i}_{1}=2\mathrm{mA}=2\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{A}$.

So, the ratio of the instantaneous voltages is:

$\frac{V_{L1}}{V_{L2}}=\frac{0.8}{0.6}=\frac{8}{6}=\frac{4}{3}$

text: The ratio of momentum of the photons of the $1^{\text{st}}$ and $2^{\text{nd}}$ line of Balmer series of Hydrogen atoms is $α/β$. The possible values of $α$ and $β$ are:-
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
According to the de Broglie relation, the momentum (p) of a photon is inversely proportional to its wavelength ( $λ$ ):

$\mathrm{p}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{λ}$

Therefore, the ratio of momenta is the inverse ratio of their wavelengths:

$\frac{\mathrm{p}_{1}}{\mathrm{p}_{2}}=\frac{λ_{2}}{λ_{1}}$

The Balmer series occurs when an electron transitions from a higher energy level $(\mathrm{n}_{2})$ to the second energy level ( $\mathrm{n}_{1}=2$ ). The wavelength is given by Rydberg formula:

$\frac{1}{λ}=\mathrm{R}\left (\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}^{2}}\right )$

For $1^{\text{st}}$ line of Balmer transition from $\mathrm{n}=3$ to $\mathrm{n}=2$.

$\frac{1}{λ_{1}}=\mathrm{R}\left (\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right )=\mathrm{R}\left (\frac{9-4}{36}\right )=\frac{5\mathrm{R}}{36}\Rightarrow λ_{1}=\frac{36}{5\mathrm{R}}$

For $2^{\mathrm{nd}}$ line of Balmer transition from $\mathrm{n}=4$ to $\mathrm{n}=2$.

$\frac{1}{λ_{2}}=\mathrm{R}\left (\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16}\right )=\mathrm{R}\left (\frac{4-1}{16}\right )=\frac{3\mathrm{R}}{16}\Rightarrow λ_{2}=\frac{16}{3\mathrm{R}}$

So, the ratio $(α/β)$,

$\frac{\mathrm{p}_{1}}{\mathrm{p}_{2}}=\frac{λ_{2}}{λ_{1}}=\frac{16/3\mathrm{R}}{36/5\mathrm{R}}=\frac{16}{3}\times \frac{5}{36}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{\mathrm{p}_{1}}{\mathrm{p}_{2}}=\frac{4\times 5}{3\times 9}=\frac{20}{27}=\frac{α}{β}$

So, $α=20$ and $β=27$.

Therefore, the correct option is (D).

text: A LCR series circuit driven with $E_{rms}=90\mathrm{V}$ at frequency $f_{\mathrm{d}}=30\mathrm{Hz}$ has resistance $R=80\Omega$, an inductance with inductive reactance $X_{L}=20.0\Omega$ and capacitance with capacitive reactance $X_{C}=80.0\Omega$. The power factor of the circuit is $____$ .
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In an AC circuit, the power factor $(\cos 𝜙)$ is defined as the ratio of the resistance $(\mathrm{R})$ to the total impedance $(\mathrm{Z})$ of the circuit :


[IMG]


$\text{Power Factor}=\cos 𝜙=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{Z}}$

For a series LCR circuit, the impedance is

$\mathrm{Z}=\sqrt{\mathrm{R}^{2}+(\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}-\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}})^{2}}$

The value of resistance is $\mathrm{R}=80\Omega$, the inductive reactance is $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}=20.0\Omega$, and the capacitive reactance is $\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}=80.0\Omega$.

$\mathrm{X}_{\text{net}}=|\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{L}}-\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{C}}|=|20-80|=60\Omega$

So, the impedance is,

$\mathrm{Z}=\sqrt{80^{2}+60^{2}}=\sqrt{6400+3600}=\sqrt{10000}=100\Omega$

Thus, the power factor is,

$\cos 𝜙=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{Z}}=\frac{80}{100}=0.8$

Therefore, the correct option is (A).

Refer to the circuit diagram given below. The heat generated across the $6\Omega$ resistance in 100 second is $\frac{α}{100}\mathrm{J}$. The value of $α$ is $____$ . (Nearest integer)

solution.body:
The heat $(H)$ generated in a resistor $(R)$ due to a current (i) flowing for a time $(t)$ is :

$\mathrm{H}=\mathrm{i}^{2}\mathrm{Rt}$

Let $V_{A}$ be the potential at the junction $A$. Using Kirchhoff's current law, the sum of currents $=0$ :


[IMG]


$\frac{V_{A}-3}{6}+\frac{V_{A}-0}{4}+\frac{V_{A}-2}{3}=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $2(V_{A}-3)+3V_{A}+4(V_{A}-2)=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $2V_{A}-6+3V_{A}+4V_{A}-8=0$

$\Rightarrow$ $9V_{A}=14\Rightarrow V_{A}=\frac{14}{9}V$

So, the current through the $6\Omega$ resistor is,

$\mathrm{i}=\frac{3-\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{A}}}{6}=\frac{3-14/9}{6}=\frac{27-14}{9\times 6}=\frac{13}{54}\mathrm{A}$

The time is $\mathrm{t}=100\mathrm{s}$.

Hence, total heat generated in $6\Omega$ is;

$H=\left (\frac{13}{54}\right )^{2}\times 6\times 100=\frac{169}{2916}\times 600\approx 34.77\mathrm{J}$

It is given that $\mathrm{H}=\frac{α}{100}$, then $α=\mathrm{H}\times 100$ :

$\Rightarrow α\approx 3477$

text: An unpolarized light of intensity $I_{0}$ passes through polarizer and then through a certain optically active solution and finally it goes to analyser. If the angle between analyser and polariser is $0^{\circ }$ and intensity of light emerged from analyser is $\frac{3}{8}I_{0}$, the angle of rotation of the light by the solution with respect to analyser is $____$ degrees.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
When unpolarized light of intensity $\mathrm{I}_{0}$ passes through a polarizer, the intensity of the transmitted polarized light $(I_{1})$ is always half of the initial intensity.

$\mathrm{I}_{1}=\frac{\mathrm{I}_{0}}{2}$

An optically active solution rotates the plane of polarization by a certain angle. Let the angle of rotation is $θ$. After passing through the solution, the light is still plane-polarized, but its axis has shifted by $θ$.

Using Malus's Law when completely plane-polarized light is incident on an analyzer, the intensity I of the light transmitted by the analyzer is directly proportional to the square of the cosine of the angle between the transmission axes of the analyzer and the polarizer.

$\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_{\text{incident}}\cos ^{2}(𝜙)$

Here, $𝜙$ is the final angle between the light's polarization plane (rotated by the solution) and the analyzer's axis.

The initial intensity after polarizer is $\mathrm{I}_{1}=\frac{\mathrm{I}_{0}}{2}$ and the final intensity after analyser is $\mathrm{I}=\frac{3}{8}\mathrm{I}_{0}$.

Since the analyzer and polarizer were originally at $0^{\circ }$, the angle $𝜙$ in Malus's law is the rotation angle $θ$ caused by the solution.

Substituting the values into Malus's Law:

$\frac{3}{8}I_{0}=\left (\frac{I_{0}}{2}\right )\cos ^{2}θ$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{3/8}{1/2}=\cos ^{2}(θ)$

$\Rightarrow$ $\frac{3}{4}=\cos ^{2}(θ)$

$\Rightarrow$ $\cos (θ)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

$\Rightarrow$ $θ=30^{\circ }$

Therefore, the angle of rotation is 30 degrees.

text: The energy released when $\frac{7}{17.13}\mathrm{kg}$ of ${}_{3}^{7}\mathrm{Li}$ is converted into ${}_{2}^{4}\mathrm{He}$ by proton bombardment is $α\times 10^{32}\mathrm{eV}$. The value of $α$ is $____$ . (Nearest integer) (Mass of ${}_{3}^{7}\mathrm{Li}=7.0183\mathrm{u}$, mass of ${}_{2}^{4}\mathrm{He}=4.004\mathrm{u}$, mass of proton $=1.008\mathrm{u}$ and $1\mathrm{u}=931\mathrm{MeV}/\mathrm{c}^{2}$ and Avogadro number $=6.0\times 10^{23}$ )
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The given reaction is the proton bombardment of lithium:

${}_{3}^{7}Li+{}_{1}^{1}p\to 2{}_{2}^{4}He$

Mass of reactants:

$m_{\text{reactants}}=m({}_{3}^{7}Li)+m({}_{1}^{1}p)=7.0183+1.008=8.0263u$

Mass of products:

$m_{\text{products}}=2\times m({}_{2}^{4}He)=2\times 4.004=8.008u$

Mass defect:

$\Delta m=m_{\text{reactants}}-m_{\text{products}}=8.0263-8.008=0.0183u$

$E_{\text{per reaction}}=\Delta m\times 931\text{MeV}$

$E_{\text{per reaction}}=0.0183\times 931=17.04\text{MeV}$

Convert this to eV:

$E_{\text{per reaction}}=17.04\times 10^{6}\text{eV}=1.704\times 10^{7}\text{eV}$

Given mass of Li:

Convert to grams:

Number of moles:

Number of atoms:

Each Li atom undergoes one reaction, so

$E_{\text{total}}=N\times E_{\text{per reaction}}$

$E_{\text{total}}=3.50\times 10^{25}\times 1.704\times 10^{7}$

$E_{\text{total}}=5.96\times 10^{32}\text{eV}$

text: A three coulomb charge moves from the point $(0,-2,-5)$ to the point $(5,1,2)$ in an electric field expressed as $⃗{E}=2x\hat{\mathrm{i}}+3\mathrm{y}^{2}\hat{\mathrm{j}}+4\hat{\mathrm{k}}\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{C}$. The work done in moving the charge is $____$ J.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The work done (W) by an external agent in moving a charge (q) in an electric field ( $\vec{\mathrm{E}}$ ) is given by the change in potential energy, which is the negative of the work done by the field.

The electric force acting on the charge by electric field is $\vec{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{q}\vec{\mathrm{E}}$

So, the work done is :

$\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{q}\int \vec{\mathrm{E}}\cdot \mathrm{d}\vec{\mathrm{r}}$

Where $\mathrm{d}\vec{\mathrm{r}}=\mathrm{dx}\text{î}+\mathrm{dy}\hat{\mathrm{j}}+\mathrm{dz}\hat{\mathrm{k}}$ is the infinitesimal displacement vector.

$\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{q}\int\limits _{(0,-2,-5)}^{(5,1,2)}\left (2\mathrm{x}\hat{ı}+3\mathrm{y}^{2}\hat{ȷ}+4\hat{\mathrm{k}}\right )\cdot (\mathrm{dx}\hat{ı}+\mathrm{dy}\hat{ȷ}+\mathrm{dz}\hat{\mathrm{k}})$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{q}\left [\int\limits _{0}^{5}2\mathrm{xdx}+\int\limits _{-2}^{1}3\mathrm{y}^{2}\mathrm{dy}+\int\limits _{-5}^{2}4\mathrm{dz}\right ]$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{q}\left [2\left [\frac{\mathrm{x}^{2}}{2}\right ]_{0}^{5}+3\left [\frac{\mathrm{y}^{3}}{3}\right ]_{-2}^{1}+4[\mathrm{x}]_{-5}^{2}\right ]$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{W}=3\left [\left [5^{2}-0^{2}\right ]+\left [1^{3}-(-2)^{3}\right ]+4[2-(-5)]\right ]$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{W}=3\times (25+9+28)$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{W}=3\times 62=186\mathrm{J}$

Therefore, the work done in moving the charge is 186 J.

text: A certain gas is isothermally compressed to $\left (\frac{1}{3}\right )^{\mathrm{rd}}$ of its initial volume $(V_{\mathrm{o}}=3$ litre) by applying required pressure. If the bulk modulus of the gas is $3\times 10^{5}\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m}^{2}$, the magnitude of work done on the gas is $____$ J.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2026 (Online) 6th April Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The Bulk Modulus of a material is defined as the ratio of the infinitesimal pressure increase (dP) to the resulting relative decrease of the volume:

$B=-\frac{dP}{dV/V}=-\frac{VdP}{dV}$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{dP}=-\mathrm{B}\frac{\mathrm{dV}}{\mathrm{V}}.$

The work done on a gas during a volume change is

$W=-\int\limits _{V_{i}}^{V_{f}}PdV$

$\Rightarrow$ $W=-\int\limits _{V_{i}}^{V_{f}}B\ln \left (\frac{V_{i}}{V}\right )dV$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{W}=\int \Delta \mathrm{P}\mathrm{dV}$

However, for a gas where B is constant during isothermal compression, the work done is:

$\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{B}\Delta \mathrm{V}$ for small changes or $\mathrm{W}=\int \mathrm{P}\mathrm{dV}$

The initial volume is $V_{i}=3$ litres $=3\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{m}^{3}$

And the final volume is $V_{f}=13\times 3=1$ litre $=1\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{m}^{3}$

So, the change in volume is;

$\Delta V=V_{i}-V_{f}=2\times 10^{-3}\mathrm{m}^{3}$

The bulk modulus is $\mathrm{B}=3\times 10^{5}\mathrm{N}/\mathrm{m}^{2}$

For an isothermal process in a gas, the Bulk Modulus is equal to the pressure ( $\mathrm{B}=\mathrm{P}$ ).

$W=\int\limits _{V_{i}}^{V_{f}}PdV=\int\limits _{V_{i}}^{V_{f}}B\frac{V_{i}}{V}dV$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{B}\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{i}}\ln \left (\frac{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{i}}}{\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{f}}}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $\mathrm{W}=\left (3\times 10^{5}\right )\times \left (3\times 10^{-3}\right )\times \ln \left (\frac{\mathrm{V}_{0}}{\mathrm{V}_{0}/3}\right )$

$\Rightarrow$ $W=900\times 1.0986\approx 988.74\mathrm{J}$

Therefore, the magnitude of work done on the gas is approximately 989 J .
